arXiv:2510.16021v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2025

Feature-driven reinforcement learning for photovoltaic in continuous intraday trading

Arega Getaneh Abate, Xiufeng Liu, Ruyu Liu, and Xiaobing Zhang Affiliation: Department of Technology, Management and Economics, Technical University of Denmark, Kgs. Lyngby, Denmark Affiliation: Affiliation: {ageab, xiuli, ruyli, xiazhan}dtu.dk Affiliation:
Abstract

Photovoltaic (PV) operators face substantial uncertainty in generation and short-term electricity prices. Continuous intraday markets enable producers to adjust their positions in real time, potentially improving revenues and reducing imbalance costs. We propose a feature-driven reinforcement learning (RL) approach for PV intraday trading that integrates data-driven features into the state and learns bidding policies in a sequential decision framework. The problem is cast as a Markov Decision Process with a reward that balances trading profit and imbalance penalties, and is solved with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) using a predominantly linear, interpretable policy. Trained on historical market data and evaluated out-of-sample, the strategy consistently outperforms benchmark baselines across diverse scenarios. Extensive validation shows rapid convergence, real-time inference, and transparent decision rules. Learned weights highlight the central role of market microstructure and historical features. Taken together, these results indicate that feature-driven RL offers a practical, data-efficient, and operationally deployable pathway for active intraday participation by PV producers.

Index Terms:
PV trading, Intraday market, Renewable energy, Forecasting, Feature-driven RL.

I Introduction

Short-term electricity markets are crucial for integrating variable renewable energy sources, such as solar photovoltaics (PV) and wind [1, 2, 3]. A common practice among PV producers is to submit day-ahead offers based on a single forecast and accept the resulting imbalances when actual generation deviates [4]. This approach is often suboptimal: forecast errors result in shortfalls or surpluses that are settled at imbalance prices, typically at a higher cost to the system and its participants. By contrast, active intraday trading enables market participants to continuously adjust their positions as forecasts are updated, thereby materially reducing final imbalances and improving financial performance [5]. Intraday markets thus provide the mechanism to incorporate late-arriving information close to delivery [6, 7, 8], which is particularly pertinent for PV with weather-driven variability.

Designing an effective intraday strategy for PV producers is nevertheless challenging. First, PV output is uncertain; forecast errors can be material even hours before delivery. Second, intraday prices are volatile and exhibit strong within-session dynamics [9]. Third, strategies must respect market microstructure, liquidity conditions, and gate-closure rules—practical constraints that shape implementability [10]. Recent Nordic market changes also impact PV trading practices, including the transition to a single-price imbalance model and the introduction of products now standard in Single Intraday Coupling (SIDC) and Single Day-ahead Coupling (SDAC)[11].

The literature tackles some of the challenges from several angles. Stochastic programming captures uncertainty in generation and prices. The authors in [2], for example, formulate a two-stage model for PV bids across day-ahead and multiple intraday rescheduling rounds, co-optimizing expected profit and risk via Conditional value at risk (CVaR). Empirical work using Danish and Nordic data demonstrates that renewable forecast errors drive systematic spreads between intraday and day-ahead prices [5]. Market-design studies show that adding intraday auctions to continuous trading can deepen liquidity and reduce volatility, directly affecting the feasibility of algorithmic strategies [10, 9]. Related hybrid intraday settings that alternate continuous and auction sessions are emerging and are explicitly modeled in recent work [12].

A second line of research integrates advanced forecasting with decision-making. Reference [1] develops a feature-driven bidding framework that feeds informative predictors into a data-driven newsvendor model, and [13] analyzes a hybrid wind power plants trading in the day-ahead market. PV-specific studies couple enhanced forecasting with operational flexibility [14].

A third strand of research applies learning-based trading. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies, including Deep Q-networks and policy-gradient methods, have been explored for intraday trading [15, 16, 17, 18]. On the other hand, the online learning approach bypasses the predict-then-optimize sequence by directly learning bidding strategies with regret guarantees [19, 20, 21].

Despite this progress, methods centered on price prediction [22] are not tailored to PV’s core competitive lever (volume forecasting) and often omit explicit co-optimization against imbalance penalties. Stochastic formulations such as [2] stop short of addressing the challenge of bidding in continuous markets. Feature-driven approaches, such as [1], focus on day-ahead under dual-price settlement, without sequential intraday updates. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work integrates data-driven features into state and learn bidding policies in sequential decisions for continuous intraday trading, explicitly models balancing-market penalties under single-price imbalance settlement, and employs a sequential, feature-driven learning strategy for PV trading.

This paper proposes an end-to-end framework for PV intraday trading that combines feature-driven forecasting and an RL algorithm that learns sequential bidding decisions in continuous intraday markets. The central premise of the paper is that augmenting RL with data-driven features about PV generation and market state yields better risk–return performance by directly managing imbalance penalties across intraday, and balancing stages. The main contributions of this work are:

  • i)

    Formulating PV intraday trading as a multistage decision problem under uncertainty and developing a mathematical model that maximizes expected profit while explicitly penalizing imbalances.

  • ii)

    Implementing a Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm with a predominantly linear policy structure that learns from historical data without requiring explicit probabilistic models of prices or generation.

  • iii)

    Designing a real-time implementable strategy that iteratively updates intraday positions as new information arrives, respecting continuous-market constraints and gate-closure rules.

  • iv)

    Validating learning dynamics, computational efficiency, and policy interpretability through systematic experiments: convergence analysis across multiple seeds, inference latency benchmarking on consumer hardware, and weight analysis revealing economic interpretability of learned trading rules.

  • v)

    Evaluating with a case study using real data from the Danish electricity market (2023–2024), showing consistent profit gains across diverse scenarios, including liquidity constraints, imbalance price shocks, and feature ablations.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the problem formulation for feature-driven PV intraday trading. Section III describes the setup of the case study and the data. It also presents the results and performance analysis, providing a discussion on the implications of our findings. Finally, Section IV concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

II Model Formulation

II-A Market Setting

To formalize the PV intraday trading problem, we first introduce the key notation in Table I. The Balancing Responsible Party (BRP) seeks to maximize the expected profit from intraday continuous (IDC) trading and balancing settlement, given fixed day-ahead (DA) commitments. We consider a planning horizon of TT delivery periods. For each delivery period, let GtD​AG^{DA}_{t} denote the PV energy committed in the day-ahead market and Gta​c​tG^{act}_{t} the realized PV generation. Any deviation Gta​c​t−GtD​AG^{act}_{t}-G^{DA}_{t} results in an imbalance that is settled in the balancing market at price PtI​MP^{IM}_{t}. Intraday continuous trades qta​s​kq^{ask}_{t} (energy sold) and qtb​u​yq^{buy}_{t} (energy purchased) allow the BRP to reduce this deviation by selling excess generation or buying energy to cover a shortfall.

We therefore maximize the expected intraday and balancing profit over the trading horizon, while penalizing trade size, residual imbalance, and deviations from a recommended policy:

II-B Feature-driven decision model

We now describe the feature-driven policy that generates the recommended intraday trading actions. Let 𝐗t∈ℝd\mathbf{X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the feature vector at time tt, and let 𝒒∈ℝd\boldsymbol{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the learned weight vector defining a linear policy. The policy’s recommended net intraday action is given by

atrec=qtask−qtbuy=𝒒⊤​𝐗t.a^{\mathrm{rec}}_{t}=q^{\mathrm{ask}}_{t}-q^{\mathrm{buy}}_{t}=\boldsymbol{q}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}. (6)

This recommendation is incorporated into the objective via the quadratic penalty term with weight κ\kappa. The optimizer is incentivized to choose intraday trades such that the net executed volume is close to 𝒒⊤​𝐗t\boldsymbol{q}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}, but it retains the flexibility to deviate when necessary. In other words, the policy suggests an action based on features, and the MIQP can override or adjust it within the limits of the constraints and for economic gain. In this work, we include five feature domains:

𝐗t=[(𝐱ttemp)⊤,(𝐱tfcst)⊤,(𝐱tmkt)⊤,(𝐱twx)⊤,(𝐱tvol)⊤,1]⊤.\mathbf{X}_{t}=\Big[(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{t})^{\top},(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{fcst}}_{t})^{\top},(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{mkt}}_{t})^{\top},(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{wx}}_{t})^{\top},(\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{vol}}_{t})^{\top},1\Big]^{\top}. (7)

Temporal features 𝐱ttemp\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{temp}}_{t} encode time-of-delivery information; forecast features 𝐱tfcst\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{fcst}}_{t} include the latest PV generation from hour t−5t-5 forecast G^t\hat{G}_{t} and recent updates or errors in the forecast; market features 𝐱tmkt\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{mkt}}_{t} include relevant price signals; weather features 𝐱twx\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{wx}}_{t} capture meteorological signals such as solar irradiance, cloud cover, which influence PV output uncertainty; and volatility features 𝐱tvol\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{vol}}_{t} quantify recent variability. We also include a constant 1 to allow an intercept term. All features are appropriately scaled for the learning algorithm.

The linear policy weight vector 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} can be structured in different ways to capture heterogeneity across time or regimes. In the training phase, the policy parameters 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} are learned from historical data. This can be formulated as finding the 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} that maximizes the total profit on the training dataset, using historical feature vectors 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and observed outcomes. In other words, we solve a learning problem to obtain 𝒒∗\boldsymbol{q}^{*} that yields a high profit when the intraday optimization (1) is executed. In the online phase, we keep 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} fixed to the learned values. At each decision time tt, we compute the recommended action atr​e​c=𝒒⊤​𝐗ta^{rec}_{t}=\boldsymbol{q}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t} from the latest features, and then solve the MIQP (1) to determine the actual intraday trade volumes qta​s​kq^{ask}_{t} and qtb​u​yq^{buy}_{t}. This two-step procedure ensures that real-time trading decisions are both adaptive and feasible in terms of market and physical constraints.

For computational efficiency within the RL training loop, we substitute the closed-form execution surrogate for repeatedly solving the MIQP. The surrogate respects the same capacity and imbalance constraints and produces the quantities qta​s​kq^{ask}_{t} and qtb​u​yq^{buy}_{t} that would be delivered to the market.

II-C RL approach for policy training

We frame the intraday trading problem as a sequential decision-making task and employ RL to train the policy parameters 𝒒\boldsymbol{q}. In this formulation, each delivery horizon can be viewed as an episode consisting of a sequence of states, actions, and rewards. The state sts_{t} at hour tt is characterized by the feature vector 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t}. The action ata_{t} is the intraday trade decision, which in our policy class corresponds to the net volume at=𝒒⊤​𝐗ta_{t}=\boldsymbol{q}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}. The immediate reward rtr_{t} is the profit achieved for hour tt as defined by the terms inside the summation of (1). The objective of the RL agent is to learn a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} that maximizes the expected cumulative reward over the episode.

To learn 𝒒\boldsymbol{q}, we adopt a policy-gradient RL algorithm, specifically a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which iteratively improves the policy by simulating trading experiences and using the observed rewards as feedback. Conceptually, the training procedure works as follows: the agent simulates many episodes using historical data. In each episode, for each period tt, the agent observes the current state 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t}, then samples an action ata_{t} according to the current policy. The intraday trading optimization is executed with that action. The agent then observes the next state and repeats this process. After completing an episode, the policy parameters are updated to increase the probability of actions that yielded higher profits and decrease the probability of suboptimal actions. Over many iterations, this process converges to a policy that maximizes the expected profit. Learning directly from data allows the agent to discover complex patterns or strategies that would be hard to derive from first principles.

The training procedure is given in Algorithm 1. In implementation, we maintain a parameter vector 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} which is updated by gradient ascent on the PPO objective. We also maintain a value function (critic) for variance reduction in estimating advantages. The Executor in the algorithm refers to solving the intraday optimization (1) given a tentative action ata_{t}, returning the actual executed volumes and the resulting reward rtr_{t}. The training involves multiple epochs of simulated rollouts over the training dataset. After convergence, the learned 𝒒\boldsymbol{q} is used for the online policy as described earlier.

II-D Feature-augmented RL for continuous intraday trading

In an intraday continuous market, a market order executes immediately against the best contra-side liquidity in the limit order book (LOB). A limit order executes only at prices no worse than its limit; any unfilled remainder rests in the LOB until expiry. If matched orders differ in size, the smaller is filled and the larger is partially filled. Figure 1 illustrates the continuous-trading mechanics (the interested reader is referred to [23]). In our model, we cast continuous intraday trading as a finite-horizon γ\gamma-discounted MDP with microstructure and imbalance risk.

We model trading as a finite-horizon γ\gamma-discounted MDP with microstructure and imbalance risk. The state

st=(xt,G^t,σt,ptDA,mt,𝝍t,𝜻t,τt)∈𝒮s_{t}=\big(x_{t},\hat{G}_{t},\sigma_{t},p^{\mathrm{DA}}_{t},m_{t},\boldsymbol{\psi}_{t},\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{t},\tau_{t}\big)\in\mathcal{S} (8)

collects inventory xtx_{t}, PV forecast and uncertainty (G^t,σt)(\hat{G}_{t},\sigma_{t}), day-ahead price ptDAp^{\mathrm{DA}}_{t}, intraday mid-price mtm_{t}, microstructure features 𝝍t\boldsymbol{\psi}_{t}, balancing-context features 𝜻t\boldsymbol{\zeta}_{t}, and time-to-delivery τt\tau_{t} (which Markovizes time). The action

at=(qt,δt)∈𝒜,qt∈[q¯,q¯],δt∈[δ¯,δ¯],a_{t}=(q_{t},\delta_{t})\in\mathcal{A},\qquad q_{t}\in[\underline{q},\overline{q}],\ \delta_{t}\in[\underline{\delta},\overline{\delta}], (9)

We regularize and optionally project toward the linear subspace for interpretability.

III Numerical experiments

III-A Data and market context

We evaluate the proposed framework in the Danish electricity market, which features a high penetration of wind and solar generation, as well as well-defined intraday and balancing mechanisms. The case study simulates a PV owner/BRP that commits day-ahead volumes based on a day-ahead forecast, updates its position in the IDC market up to shortly before delivery as information improves, and settles any residual deviation in the balancing market.

We use hourly data from 2023 to 2024. The dataset includes day-ahead clearing prices PtDAP^{\mathrm{DA}}_{t} and committed volumes GtDAG^{\mathrm{DA}}_{t}, intraday continuous market prices (PtID,bid,PtID,ask)(P^{\mathrm{ID,bid}}_{t},P^{\mathrm{ID,ask}}_{t}), imbalance prices PtIMP^{\mathrm{IM}}_{t}, system up/down regulation status, measured PV generation GtactG^{\mathrm{act}}_{t}, and intraday PV production forecasts, including t−5t-5 hours lags. All time series are synchronized to hourly delivery periods for consistency, even though the IDC market supports sub-hourly trading. Day-ahead prices and PV-related time series are sourced from [24]. Continuous intraday trading records (Elbas) and depth snapshots (bid/ask volumes) are taken from [25]. Gas balancing prices are used as the basis for the imbalance penalty surrogate. After processing all raw data through a single pipeline, the combined series yields 17,369 hourly observations spanning January 2023 through December 2024. Synthetic intraday bid/ask quotes and depth bounds are then derived from the day-ahead price spread and the observed countertrade volumes, providing the execution parameters used by the RL environment. The resulting panel is split chronologically: January-December 2023 is used for training, and January-December 2024 serves as the out-of-sample evaluation set.

Generation is represented by a 10 MW PV plant parameterized to Danish conditions (annual capacity factor 12.5%12.5\%, typical for latitude ∼55.7∘\sim 55.7^{\circ}N). Forecast errors are calibrated to empirical magnitudes: day-ahead forecast standard deviation ≈15%\approx 15\% of capacity and intraday updates ≈8%\approx 8\%. Meteorological features are obtained from the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI) at hourly resolution and spatially interpolated to the plant site [26]. We include global horizontal irradiance, satellite-derived cloud cover, and 2m air temperature, both directly and through engineered features that capture diurnal and seasonal structure, to inform forecasts and uncertainty.

For each delivery hour tt, we construct a feature vector 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} from information available up to a cutoff one hour before delivery. Specifically, by t−1t{-}1 h the BRP observes a final intraday forecast for GtactG^{\mathrm{act}}_{t}, the current IDC quotes, and recent imbalance price dynamics.

To emulate continuous intraday trading, we simulate depth-aware execution against best quotes and a stylized order book. Market orders incur a spread-scaled linear cost plus a convex depth penalty. Limit orders placed at an offset δt\delta_{t} fill according to a calibrated probability model that depends on observed bid/ask volumes and recent order flow. Time steps are refined near gate closure to reflect increased trading intensity and more frequent forecast updates. This setup preserves tractability while capturing the essential maker-taker and liquidity trade-offs faced by PV traders in practice. Residual deviations at delivery are settled at PtIMP^{\mathrm{IM}}_{t}.

III-B Experimental design and simulation results

III-B1 Model training and benchmarking

We train the feature-driven PPO agent on data from January 2023 to December 2023 and evaluate it out-of-sample on calendar year 2024. Training is conducted at the daily granularity: each episode consists of 24 intraday trading rounds, followed by a policy update. To reduce sensitivity to random initialization, we run five independent seeds (17, 29, 41, 53, 67); each seed executes six PPO epochs with 1,024 environment steps per epoch. The discount factor is set to γ=0.98\gamma=0.98, and the initial policy mean is zero so that exploration noise and gradient updates jointly shape the coefficients.

After training, the learned weights are frozen and deployed in 2024 without further adaptation. Every result below reports the mean across the five seeds together with the half-width of the 95% confidence interval (CI), thereby reflecting both seed-to-seed variability and stochasticity in the simulated execution model.

We benchmark the feature-driven RL policy (FDRL) against four practical alternatives with identical pre-processing and execution assumptions: (i) a spot-only strategy that clears the full forecast day-ahead and absorbs deviations in balancing; (ii) a forecast-tracking rule that trades exactly the forecast error Δ​G^t\Delta\hat{G}_{t} regardless of prices; (iii) a sign/spread heuristic that trades toward Δ​G^t\Delta\hat{G}_{t} only when the simulated spread is sufficiently narrow; and (iv) a perfect-foresight oracle that knows realized generation and prices in advance and therefore provides an upper bound on attainable profit. Figure 2 presents a visual comparison of FDRL against all baselines across profit, risk-adjusted performance, trading activity, and tail risk metrics. For reproducibility, all code, configuration files, and experiment logs are available at the repository in [27].

III-B2 Performance across stress scenarios

Table II summarises the 2024 out-of-sample results. Profits and tail-risk measures are reported in thousands of euros; parentheses denote the 95% confidence interval half-width across the five training seeds, and the right-most columns list the mean number of trades and the estimated 5% CVaR of daily profits.

Figure 3 visualizes these outcomes. We group the scenarios to highlight how each stressor affects profit, activity, and tail risk (CVaR5%):

  • •

    Baseline. The feature-driven policy (FDRL) delivers a positive uplift of 1.53 k€  (0.5%) over spot-only with a mean trade count of 41. The reported CI half-width (4.71) reflects seed variability and execution stochasticity, but the uplift is positive across runs.

  • •

    Liquidity scaling. Cutting available depth to 50% or 25% preserves similar uplifts (1.59–1.86 k€ ) with only a small increase in trades (to 43). CVaR remains close to baseline. This suggests the policy’s profitability does not rely on unrealistically deep books and that the execution surrogate’s depth penalties are not the bottleneck in these regimes.

  • •

    Imbalance price shocks. When shortage penalties rise (+1​σ+1\sigma), uplift shrinks to 0.58 k€  and the tail worsens (CVaR −0.058-0.058), while softer penalties (−1​σ-1\sigma) increase uplift to 2.70 k€  with benign tails. This aligns with incentives: harsher imbalance pricing leaves less room for profitable intraday corrections before delivery.

  • •

    Feature ablations. Removing meteorological features flips the uplift negative (−3.31-3.31 k€ ) despite similar activity (39 trades), indicating that weather context is critical for deciding when to intervene. Excluding liquidity features increases activity (47 trades) and slightly raises mean uplift (to 1.91 k€ ) but with a worse tail (CVaR −0.039-0.039), consistent with a more aggressive stance when depth signals are absent. Removing market features in this run leaves the mean profit near the baseline but increases activity (58 trades), which we interpret as less selective trading when the price context is suppressed. The learned policy weights (Figure 4, right panel) reveal that market microstructure features (bid/ask depth, prices) and forecast signals carry the highest absolute weights, confirming these domains dominate trading decisions.

  • •

    Forecast horizon swaps. Faster forecasts materially raise value: using a 1 h horizon yields the largest uplift (4.31 k€ ) alongside the highest activity (65 trades). The tail is not a -0.176), signaling a risk–return trade-off from acting more frequently on rapidly changing information. With 5 h or day-ahead horizons, uplifts remain positive (2.35 k€  and 1.81 k€ ) and tails are close to baseline.

  • •

    Risk-aversion sweep. Varying CVaR shaping (α∈{0.7,0.9,0.95}\alpha\in\{0.7,0.9,0.95\}) leaves mean profit essentially unchanged (311.95–312.01 k€ ) and tails tightly clustered (−0.020-0.020 to −0.018-0.018), indicating that the learned policy is already conservative and additional tail-weighting mostly trims marginal gains.

These results support three takeaways: (i) FDRL’s gains are robust to plausible liquidity constraints; (ii) weather and price context are consequential for timing interventions; and (iii) shorter-horizon forecasts unlock higher uplifts at the expense of fatter left tails unless risk is controlled.

III-B3 Trading behavior and learning dynamics

The learned policy intervenes selectively. In the baseline scenario, it executes on roughly 39 hours per month, trimming residual imbalances by about 3% relative to spot-only. Liquidity stress increases activity to at most 45- 70 hours per month, while the one-hour forecast configuration raises both trade count and profit in line with the richer information set. Even in the most active cases, the policy trades fewer than nine times per day on average, confirming that the additional profit stems from targeted realignment of the position rather than wholesale churning of the intraday book. Figure 5 provides a detailed analysis of the learned trading behavior, showing the hourly activity distribution, action space utilization, and revealing a preference for conservative limit orders. Additionally, it presents the trade size distribution, with a median executed volume of 3.3 MWh.

Figure 6 presents the training convergence analysis across five independent random seeds. The PPO algorithm converges within six epochs, with episode returns stabilizing after approximately four epochs of training. The mean return trajectory shows consistent improvement with low inter-seed variance, demonstrating robust learning behavior. The policy loss decreases from an initial value of approximately 0.04 to near-zero levels, while maintaining stable estimates of the value function. This rapid convergence, requiring fewer than 30,000 environment interactions per seed, confirms the sample efficiency of the feature-driven approach. The final policies exhibit return standard deviations of approximately 5.1 million euros across episodes, reflecting the inherent variability in market conditions and PV generation patterns. All five seeds achieve convergence without signs of instability or divergence, supporting the reliability of the training procedure for practical deployment.

III-B4 Computational efficiency

Table III reports inference latency measurements on consumer-grade hardware (Intel CPU, no GPU acceleration). The FDRL policy achieves a mean decision latency of 0.038 ms, with a 99th-percentile latency of 0.068 ms, which is well within the real-time requirements for hourly trading decisions. Full episode execution (24 hourly decisions) completes in 2.3 ms on average, yielding a throughput of 438 episodes per second. For comparison, hourly trading rounds provide a decision budget of approximately 60 seconds, meaning the agent operates nearly one million times faster than the minimum requirement. Training time for the baseline configuration is under 1 hour on standard hardware for six epochs. These results confirm that the learned policy is computationally lightweight and readily deployable in operational settings without requiring specialized infrastructure. The sub-millisecond inference latency also leaves ample headroom for incorporating additional pre-processing, ensemble methods, or safety checks in a production pipeline.

III-B5 Policy interpretability

Table IV presents the learned linear policy weights, sorted by absolute magnitude. The volume action assigns the highest weights to intraday ask prices (−0.216-0.216), indicating reduced volume with higher prices, bid depth (+0.210+0.210), indicating more volume with deeper books, and forecast uncertainty (−0.207-0.207). The delta (aggressiveness) action shows sensitivity to bid depth (+0.204+0.204), forecast level (−0.162-0.162, suggesting more conservative trading when expected generation is high), and total market depth (+0.155+0.155). The negative weight on forecast level aligns with risk management intuitions: when expected generation is high, the policy becomes less aggressive to avoid overcommitting.

The predominantly linear structure facilitates direct interpretation: each weight quantifies the marginal influence of a standardized feature on the corresponding action dimension. The signed weights reveal economically sensible patterns. For example, higher imbalance prices reduce trading volume (−0.190-0.190), while deeper markets encourage both trading volume and aggressiveness. Across both actions, the top five features account for 35–45% of the total weight magnitude, indicating that while the policy leverages the full feature set. A small number of key predictors, particularly market microstructure (depth, prices) and forecast signals, dominate decision-making. This interpretability supports auditability and regulatory compliance, as operators can trace trading decisions back to observable market conditions and physical signals. The learned weights remain stable across training seeds (standard deviation <<0.05 for top features), further confirming the robustness of the feature-driven approach.

IV Conclusion and future work

This paper presented a comprehensive study on strategic intraday trading for a PV power producer, aimed at maximizing profit while minimizing imbalance costs. We formulated the intraday trading problem as a sequential decision optimization and introduced a feature-driven reinforcement learning approach that leverages real-time data and domain features to make optimal trading decisions. The method enables a PV operator to continuously adjust its position in the intraday market as new information becomes available, thereby reducing its reliance on imperfect day-ahead forecasts.

Across various market conditions, the feature-driven policy consistently delivers a significant uplift over spot-only trading. CVaR remains tightly clustered, indicating that improvements are not obtained by loading additional tail risk. Methodologically, the controller is prescriptive and lightweight: it learns directly from realized intraday profit and imbalance penalties using familiar hourly forecasts and price feeds, without requiring calibrated probabilistic models. The predominantly linear policy remains interpretable; learned weights suggest market microstructure and weather signals dominate decisions. Operationally, the policy intervenes sparingly, yet residual imbalances decline versus the spot-only benchmark, consistent with targeted realignment rather than wholesale re-hedging. By learning adaptive policies on standard BRP data feeds, it narrows the gap between perfect-foresight benchmarks and real-world operations under uncertainty, supporting more efficient integration of variable renewables. Limitations include a stylized execution layer calibrated to depth snapshots and spreads (abstracting strategic order-book interactions and venue heterogeneity), a one-year out-of-sample evaluation (2024) after training on 2023 data, hourly proxies for imbalance settlement, and a focus on a single 10 MW PV asset with exogenous day-ahead commitments. Performance under different weather regimes, regulatory changes, or structural shifts warrants further study.

Future work could include (i) portfolio-level control and aggregation across assets with explicit risk objectives (e.g., CVaR) in training, (ii) richer execution models and market-design analyses (gate-closure rules, liquidity incentives, imbalance pricing), (iii) multi-agent settings to capture strategic BRP interactions, and coupling with physical models such as hybrid PV–storage and degradation-aware dispatch to assess system-level benefits.
